title: Burst-rate sanitizer incident scratchpad
content:
Context:
I noticed a sustained QPS drop on the hosted API on 2025-11-01 that correlated with a config rollout for the new smoothing policy in the request-rate-sanitizer. This doc is a personal scratchpad of commands, logs, quick checks, and hypotheses (messy). Goal: capture breadcrumbs so we can triage faster and avoid blaming infra when it was a config issue.

What I observed (high level):
- Clients with steady low-latency request streams suddenly saw p50/p95 stable but p99 and overall successful tokens-per-second for the service fell ~30% during 08:10-09:30 UTC.
- Spike in queued requests flagged by the worker metrics (queue_len per shard) followed by a cascading backpressure.
- Batcher logs show frequent small-window flushes instead of expected continuous assembly -> more overhead per token.

Quick live checks I ran (timestamps local to my tickets):
- metric snapshot (promql):
  sum(rate(redwood_inference_tokens_processed_total[1m])) by (model)
  -> baseline 420k tps -> dropped to ~290k tps during incident window

- check active smoothing policy config (api):
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://controlplane.internal/v1/policies/sanitizer/current | jq .
  -> returned smoothing:{"enabled":true,"type":"exponential","alpha":1.2,"burst_threshold":0.6}  <-- alpha>1 looks suspicious

- pod logs from batcher (filtered):
  kubectl logs -n inference batcher-7c9f5 -c batcher --since=2h | sed -n '1,200p'
  --- snippets ---
  2025-11-01T08:12:14Z batcher INFO windowed_flush: assembled_window size=4 duration_ms=3
  2025-11-01T08:12:15Z batcher WARN flush_early: reason=policy_override smoothing_factor=1.2
  2025-11-01T08:12:15Z batcher INFO emit_batch: tokens=56 latency_ms=2
  2025-11-01T08:12:16Z batcher INFO windowed_flush: assembled_window size=32 duration_ms=18
  2025-11-01T08:12:16Z sanitizer WARN drop_if_burst: measured_burst=0.75 threshold=0.6 action=scale_down
  2025-11-01T08:12:16Z sanitizer INFO rate_adjust: applied_smoothing=1.2 target_batch_window_ms=10

- observed log pattern: sanitizer frequently emits scale_down when measured_burst > threshold, then batcher short-circuits to smaller windows. That increases per-request overhead and reduces token throughput.

Commands I used to reproduce locally (dev cluster):
- replay a 500rps trace from prod for 3 minutes with env var ENABLE_SANITIZER=1/0:
  python tools/replay_trace.py --trace traces/prod-2025-11-01-08.trace --qps 500 --duration 180 --env ENABLE_SANITIZER=1
  -> with sanitizer enabled + alpha=1.2 saw throughput collapse to ~65% baseline.
  -> with sanitizer disabled or alpha=0.3 recovered to baseline.

- inspect sanitizer code quick grep (branch: feature/smoothing):
  git grep "smoothing" -n runtime/sanitizer | sed -n '1,200p'
  -> smoothing uses formula: adjusted = measured * pow(alpha, measured)  (alpha default 0.9 pre-rollback)
  -> alpha>1 can amplify measured burst instead of smoothing it (bug/poor-config)

Error snippets and oddities captured:
- logs: "sanitizer WARN drop_if_burst: measured_burst=0.75 threshold=0.6 action=scale_down" (scale_down triggers immediate per-shard qps cap)
- metrics: redwood_sanitizer_scale_events_total spiked from 0 -> 240 in 10m window
- alert: "model tokens/sec fell below expected for >5m" fired and was paged (no CPU/host issue indicated)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Configuration regression: smoothing alpha accidentally set >1 in rollout (most likely). This turns a smoothing filter into an amplifier for measured bursts which causes sanitizer to over-react.
2) Measurement skew: the measured_burst calc uses a short window and is picking up normal microbursts; combined with alpha>1 produces false positives.
3) Interaction with autoscaler: sanitizer scale_down reduced effective concurrency so autoscaler sees lower CPU and removes instances (unlikely but possible given timing).
4) Hidden fallback: when sanitizer scales down it triggers the per-request fallback path that avoids async batching, increasing latency and reducing throughput.

Temporary mitigation performed:
- rolled back smoothing policy to previous version (alpha=0.9) at 08:42 UTC (controlplane rollback).
- observed tps recover to ~98% of baseline by 08:48 UTC.
- created a short-lived feature flag to disable sanitizer for customers hit (FF: sanitizer_override for customer groups).

Longer-term fixes to propose:
- enforce safe bounds in control plane UI and API for smoothing alpha (0.5 <= alpha <= 1.0). Reject values outside range.
- change default measured_burst window to geometric mean of last 3 windows to reduce sensitivity to microbursts.
- add unit + property tests for smoothing behavior with alpha<1, alpha==1, alpha>1 to prevent regression.
- add an AB test and gradual rollout guard (server-side canary) that monitors tokens/sec and avoids global rollout if delta > 5%

Notes to self (TODOs):
- postmortem stub: INF-2147 (link above) -> fill timeline and attach traces.
- pair with Priya to add a regression test in CI that replays the prod trace and asserts tps delta < 5%.
- check autoscaler logs around 08:20-08:50 to confirm whether instances were removed in response to scale_down metrics (kubectl get hpa -n inference).
- follow up with eng-console to add a warning when policy alpha > 1 is submitted via UI/CLI.

Random commands/code excerpts I saved:
- quick sanity curl to controlplane to set safe alpha (one-liner):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    https://controlplane.internal/v1/policies/sanitizer -d '{"smoothing": {"enabled": true, "alpha": 0.9, "burst_threshold": 0.6}}'

- small python snippet I used to test smoothing math quickly:
  def smooth(measured, alpha):
      return measured * (alpha ** measured)
  for a in [0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2]:
      print(a, smooth(0.6, a))

Observations when testing: smooth(0.6,1.2) -> 0.6 * (1.2**0.6) = 0.71 (amplifies)

Bottom line (notes for pager team):
- Do not assume sanitizer config is purely protective. A bad parameter can flip it into an amplifier. Guardrails needed.
- For immediate triage: check controlplane policy alpha, scan recent policy rollouts for alpha>1, and if found rollback to prior safe value.

End of scratchpad. Keep this for postmortem timeline and attach log snippets and the replay trace.
